- **Number of layers.** "One to two very thin layers" of paint.
  One canvas: primings 1–3, underdrawing, underpainting, one smalt paint
  layer, egg white, then later varnishes. Another: a first
  dark-blue layer, then light blue, pink and white in places.
  A third: "a single thin layer using remarkably few pigments".
  A fourth (1807/08): two ocher ground layers, a patchy white ground, a
  thin violet layer (smalt splinters and cinnabar), then a very thin
  pale-yellow layer.
- **Film thickness.** "Very, very fine layers"; a "gossamer-thin
  film".
- **Pooling.** The thin paint "accumulated in the depths of the textured
  ground layers," producing the finest dots of color and "almost
  continuous gradations" without visible brushstrokes.
- **Stippling.** Some passages are stippled, which "enhance[s] the
  transparency and light scattering".
- **Strokes.** Early brushwork is "painstaking… small strokes of paint
  placed side by side like a closely woven textile". Paint
  was modeled while still wet.
- **Impasto.** Limited in early works; some later works mix thick
  and thin paint and leave the ground bare in places.
- **Order of work.** Ground (bought), then underdrawing, then a "very thin
  underpainting," then paint; small details were added last,
  over finished passages.

## 7. Condition and aging

- **Fragility.** The thin paint made the paintings "exceptionally prone to
  damage"; many micro-losses come from abrasion in past
  cleaning.
- **Smalt discoloration.** Smalt has partly lost its color in one painting:
  low potassium (4.9 wt%) and changed cobalt coordination show an
  intermediate stage of degradation; a simulation of the original colors
  comes out cooler and bluer. Smalt can turn brown over
  time.
- **Craquelure.** One painting has an elongated craquelure, probably from
  pressure on the back.
- **Pentimenti.** Few.

## 8. Greens

- **Mostly mixed.** The Dresden team (14 paintings) writes that "the
  palette was very sparing" but the greens show a "lush variety"
  ("üppige Vielfalt"). The true greens were "copper-containing pigments
  and green earth." Greens were often mixed from blue and yellow: Prussian
  blue "very often," smalt and cobalt blue as well, with yellow ocher,
  Naples yellow or chrome yellow. Green passages often have
  "several (up to four) layers of different greens".
- **One painting of 1808.** Copper and arsenic were found in the same
  green layer of *Bohemian Landscape with Mount Milešovka*. The Dresden
  researchers interpret this as a degraded copper-arsenic green.
- **Rinmann's green**, rare, found on three paintings of about 1819–23.
- **A dating test.** A painting was de-attributed partly because its greens
  are cobalt blue mixed with chrome yellow, anachronistic for its supposed
  date of 1798/99.

| Green | Date and availability |
| --- | --- |
| Green earth (terre verte) | Ancient; in painters' manuals through the 19th century |
| Verdigris / copper resinate | Old; "rarely found in eighteenth- and nineteenth-century paintings"; around 1816 still made as green "varnishes" |
| Scheele's green (copper arsenite) | "Introduced in 1778"; "use as an artist's pigment is little documented" |
| Schweinfurt/emerald green | Made from 1814; a trade secret until 1822; sold in tubes from 1832; earliest easel finds c.1832 |
| Rinmann's green (cobalt-zinc oxide) | 1780; "poor tinting strength and high cost… kept it in limited use" |
| Chromium oxide (opaque) | "Rarely used because of its high price" (1831); earliest finds 1845–50 |
| Viridian | Made c.1838, patented 1859, earliest finds 1863 |
| Chrome green (chrome yellow + Prussian blue) | Appeared shortly after chrome yellow; chrome yellow made commercially in Germany only from 1820 |

Green earth is translucent, weak and short of body.

## 9. The tubes here

The supplied box contains lead white, smalt, pale smalt, yellow ochre,
red earth, vermilion, raw umber, bone black, cobalt blue, chrome yellow,
Prussian blue, green earth, Rinmann's green, copper green, Naples yellow
and rose madder: a selection
from materials documented across Friedrich's career. Ochers and yellow
earths correspond to yellow ochre; red earths and red iron oxide to red
earth; cinnabar to vermilion. The supplied copper green is verdigris
ground in oil.

Naples yellow is lead antimonate. The supplied red lake is rose madder,
a madder lake on alumina. The easel guide lists each tube's
properties.

## 10. At this easel

- **Support.** Plain-weave linen with layered grounds laid from the tubes.
  Knife application levels the weave; roller and brush application leave
  their own fine texture. The preparation is dry when painting starts.
- **Drawing.** Graphite pencils, black chalk and ruled lines.
- **Paint.** Tube mixtures can be ground in linseed, walnut or poppy oil.
  Added oil makes a mixture more transparent and fluid. `turps=` thins it
  with solvent that evaporates as the paint is laid; `thinner=` leaves
  solvent in the film to evaporate over painting time. The guide describes
  both methods.
- **Taking paint off.** Brushes pick up wet paint as they pass. A rag
  wipes or blots wet paint; a painting knife scrapes it with its blade.
- **Everything else** the easel does is in the easel guide.

# Physics of oil paint on canvas

**Tags.** **[V]**: the number is in the source text. **[S]**: the number is from a summary of the source. **[E]**: an estimate or derivation, with its assumptions stated.

---

## 1. Rheology and leveling

**Constitutive behavior.** Tube oil paint is a viscoplastic, shear-thinning and thixotropic suspension. A Herschel–Bulkley law fits it well: τ = τ_y + K·γ̇ⁿ, with n ≈ 0.2–0.7[S].

| Quantity | Value | Tag |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Yield stress, model ultramarine oil paint (32 vol% solids) | **10–20 Pa**. Brushstrokes came out regular and low-relief (Rz < 100 µm) | [V] |
| Yield stress, same paint + 4 vol% egg yolk (capillary network) | **≈3000–3200 Pa**. Strong impasto, and wrinkling suppressed | [V] |
| Typical tube paints | ~10–1000 Pa; stiff impasto grades above 1000 Pa | [S] |
| Apparent viscosity | 10⁴–10⁷ Pa·s at 0.01–0.1 s⁻¹; 10–10³ Pa·s at 10–100 s⁻¹ (brushing) | [S] |
| Linseed oil (the medium) | η ≈ 0.048 Pa·s, σ ≈ 33–36 mN/m at 20 °C | [S] |
| Stand oil | η ≈ 0.5–25 Pa·s depending on grade | [S] |

Impasto requires "sufficiently high yield stress preventing levelling after brush passage," while brushability depends on the *high-shear* viscosity, so stiff paint can still brush easily[V].

**Orchard leveling (Newtonian, thin film h ≪ λ).** A sinusoidal ridge of wavelength λ on a film of mean thickness h decays as a(t) = a₀·e^(−t/τ), with

  **τ = 3η(λ/2π)⁴ / (σh³)**[V].

The dependence is λ⁴ and h⁻³, so λ and h matter far more than η or σ.

**Yield-stress floor.** Surface tension produces a leveling stress of about 8π³σha/λ³. Flow stops once τ_y exceeds it, so ridges smaller than

  **a_c = τ_y λ³ / (8π³ σ h)**

stay frozen[S]. For thixotropic paint, τ_y(t) recovers after brushing, so leveling starts and then freezes with a residual mark[S]. With solvent evaporation, moderate yield stress can reduce residual unevenness[S].

**Worked numbers [E]** (σ = 0.035 N/m):

| Case | η | λ | h | τ (1/e time) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Medium-rich glaze, bristle striation | 1 Pa·s | 0.3 mm | 20 µm | 0.06 s |
| Glaze, stroke-scale ridge | 1 Pa·s | 2 mm | 20 µm | 110 s |
| Tube paint, stroke ridge, low-shear η | 10³–10⁴ Pa·s | 2 mm | 100 µm | 15 min – 2.5 h |

| τ_y | Frozen amplitude a_c, λ = 0.3 mm, h = 100 µm | a_c, λ = 2 mm, h = 300 µm |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 15 Pa | ~0.5–1 µm | ~45 µm |
| 100 Pa | ~3–6 µm | ~300 µm |
| 500 Pa | ~15–30 µm | effectively frozen |
| 3000 Pa | ~90–200 µm | frozen |

The ranges come from comparing the thin-film form with a deep-layer form, a_c ≈ τ_yλ²/(4π²σ), derived for h ≳ λ/2π, where the lubrication assumption fails [E]. **Inferred for this case:** at the example's λ = 0.3 mm and h = 100 µm, the estimated arrest amplitude rises from about 0.5–1 µm at 15 Pa to about 3–6 µm at 100 Pa. Retained relief depends on wavelength, thickness, initial amplitude and recovering rheology, so no single yield stress marks where striations become visible. The Newtonian glaze example predicts that fine striations level quickly. Which marks stay visible also depends on conditions these calculations leave out.

## 2. Brush marks

| Fiber | Diameter | Tip | Tag |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Hog bristle | 0.20–0.30 mm (fine hog 0.15–0.25) | Naturally split ("flagged") | [S] |
| Kolinsky/red sable | ~60–120 µm | Single fine taper | [S] |

In profilometry of oil paintings, the height features that best identify the painter sit at **0.2–0.4 mm**, matching the bristle widths used (**0.25 and 0.65 mm**)[V]. For macro impasto, a 17th-century canvas has measured relief up to about 0.85 mm[S].

**Dry brush and scumble.** A technical description of an 1879/80 canvas reports "an almost dry brush [dragged] across the surface, catching only the thread tops". This works even over a heavy, smooth ground: the paint goes where the brush touches.

## 3. Film formation and drying

- **Mass and skin timeline.** A titanium white in alkali-refined linseed oil (10 mil ≈ 250 µm film) gained nearly **16%** of its oil weight in the first days. It "begins to skin over" as it nears the peak and is touch-dry at **4–6 days**. Cold-pressed and alkali-refined oils peak at **15–18%** and then slowly lose mass over a year or more[V].
- **Thickness.** Thicker oil-paint films generally take longer to dry. Drying also depends on pigment, oil and additives. The easel guide describes drying in this studio.
- **Induction.** Drying oils take up oxygen only after an induction period; driers shorten it or speed the uptake. Lead white alone barely speeds the oxidation of linseed oil, and its impurities (litharge, lead acetate) probably account for its reputation as a drier[S].
- **Skinning and wrinkling.** Oxygen enters through the surface, so a crosslinked skin forms over mobile paint. Wrinkling is a compressive buckle of that skin. It is worse in thick, oil-rich or drier-heavy films[V]. Raising τ_y to about 3200 Pa suppressed wrinkling in model paints[V].
- **Long-term shrinkage and brittleness** (films 21–31 years old, cold-pressed linseed oil)[S]:

| Paint | Cumulative shrinkage | Aged strain at break | Aged modulus |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Lead white | 0.5% | 0.3–0.8% | ~1 GPa |
| Lead white + litharge | 0.9% | 0.5% | ~2.9 GPa |
| Zinc white | 0.3% | 0.1–0.3% | 2–3 GPa |
| Verdigris | 1.7% | 0.1% | — |
| Red iron oxide | ~0% | 0.3% | ~50 MPa |

  Lead white's strain at break fell from **7.3% at 0.2 years** to under 1% at 31 years[S]. Chalk-glue grounds are modeled with a break strain of **0.002**[V].
- **Layer thicknesses.** A three-layer commercial ground from about 1880 measured **1.5–30 µm (chalk), 5–35 µm and 10–45 µm (lead white)**[V]. Mock-up oil layers measured **59–125 µm for one coat** and 110–188 µm for two[S]. Single paint layers run roughly 10–200+ µm [S; general cross-section ranges, low confidence].
- **Conformal or filling.** That ground is "thicker and smoother, greatly diminishing the texture of the canvas weave"[V]. In the Newtonian free-surface model, thinner films level more slowly at fixed viscosity and wavelength, because τ ∝ h⁻³. At η = 1 Pa·s and σ = 0.035 N/m, λ = 0.3–0.8 mm and h = 10–20 µm give 1/e times of about 0.056–22.5 seconds, which can be fast compared with drying. Whether weave relief survives depends on viscosity, yield stress, contact during application and drying, as well as on film thickness[E].

## 4. Canvas and ground

**Thread counts (plain weave unless noted).** These are measurements of individual paintings, not period averages.

| Canvas | Threads/cm | Tag |
| --- | --- | --- |
| French 18th-century hemp | mostly 12–14 × 9.5–13 | [V] |
| French 18th century, hemp warp and linen weft | 17 × 14 | [V] |
| French 19th century | 10 × 6 (coarse) to 16 × 10 | [V] |
| Twill linen, 1830 | 30 × 29 | [V] |
| Fine linen, 1855 | 38 × 34 | [V] |
| Commercial canvas, 1879/80 | 26.0 × 29.9 | [V] |
| Commercial roll (Tasset et L'Hôte), 1888–90 | ~12 × 15–17 (e.g., 12.3 × 17.3) | [S] |

A usable range for 19th-century canvases is **10–38 threads/cm**, which is a **0.26–1.0 mm pitch**. Warp and weft often differ by 10–40%.

- **Irregularity.** Density along the warp is always more consistent than along the weft[V]. Weft "slubs" (thick spots) are the usual irregularity[S].
- **Cusping (scalloping).** This is "a regular scalloping of the threads at the perimeter" left by the tacks used while the canvas was sized and grounded[V]. On the 1879/80 canvas the original tacks were **5.5–6 cm apart**[V]. Commercial pre-primed rolls often show *no* cusping on edges cut from the roll[V].
- **Ground and texture.** Late-19th-century commercial grounds were either *à grain* (one layer, so more weave texture shows) or *lisse* (two layers, fills the interstices)[S]. An **estimate is 5–40 µm** peak to valley under *à grain* and about 2–10 µm under *lisse* **[E, unverified]**.
- **Mechanics.** Above about 80% RH the canvas *shrinks* as crimp increases, and once dry the glue size, not the canvas, carries the tension[V].

content.thinking:
I'm browsing through Caspar David Friedrich's famous works, considering pieces like Wanderer above the Sea of Fog, Monk by the Sea, and Chalk Cliffs on Rügen as possible inspiration.

I want to invent something original rather than copy a specific painting, so I'm sketching out ideas: a dusk marsh scene with a glowing yellow-rose sky fading into deep blue, a bare oak silhouette, and a Rückenfigur couple watching a crescent moon reflected in channel water -- combining elements from The Large Enclosure and Two Men Contemplating the Moon. I'm also considering a Baltic shoreline with figures on dark rocks watching ships arrive under a rising moon.

I'm settling on "Evening on the Elbe marshes" -- a vast graduated sky from warm ivory at the horizon through pale green into deep smalt blue, a thin moon, a dark foreground mound with a gnarled dead oak and a lone figure leaning on a staff, with flat meadowland stretching beyond.

I briefly consider a simpler alternative, layered mountain ridges in morning fog reminiscent of Wanderer above the Sea of Fog, but decide the twilight oak-and-figure composition is more compelling despite the challenge of rendering the tree's gnarled branch structure against the smooth gradient sky Friedrich was known for. Now I'm working out the actual canvas dimensions and composition, picking a landscape format around 70 x 50 cm with the horizon placed low, roughly 62% down the frame.

Sky takes up about two-thirds of the canvas with horizon at y≈470 of 714. I'm placing a dark rising hillock at the bottom carrying a dead oak off-center-left, a lone figure at its crest seen from behind, a silvery marsh beyond reflecting the horizon's light, and a distant town silhouette with a church spire fading into blue haze. The sky gradates from warm pale rose-yellow at the horizon through pale green to deep smalt blue above, with a thin crescent moon and evening star placed high right. I debate adding a second figure but decide solitude suits Friedrich better, then start wondering whether the tree is even necessary or if a different foreground element would work better.

Settling on keeping the oak, figure, and marsh, I'm considering putting the thin crescent moon lower in the sky near the warm-to-blue transition with a star beside it, similar to Friedrich's "Two Men Contemplating the Moon." For the ground preparation I'm planning a warm underlayer of red earth and ochre applied with a knife, then a lighter lead-white layer brushed over it so the warm striations show through.

For the construction itself, I'm starting with a graphite underdrawing establishing the horizon, tree, and figure, then thin underpainting followed by thin paint layers. I want the sky gradient built through blended piles whose weights vary with vertical position, since that's a legitimate blending gesture rather than computing an image directly into the masks.

Though actually, it might be more authentic to lay horizontal bands of separately mixed piles with a broad brush and blend them wet with a badger brush, the way real painters grade skies — I should test this on scratch and check my references on tree structure, oil blending, glazes, and grounds first.

{"id": "tree-structure", "title": "Tree structure and species", "page": 1, "pages": 4, "next_page": 2, "text": "# Trees: how they are built

*A note on how trees grow, branch and taper, from documented sources. "General knowledge" marks statements not tied to a source; "My inference" marks conclusions drawn from sourced facts.*

## In short

1. **A tree is a branching system that grows at its tips and thickens everywhere.** Strong side branches arise mostly near the top of each year's shoot (acrotony). Upright axes build the frame; side axes spread sideways. When a tip dies, the one or more side shoots below it take over, so the axis forks or zigzags.
2. **Diameter is conserved across forks, roughly.** The cross-section below a fork about equals the sum of the cross-sections above it (the branch-area rule). The measured exponent is 1.8–2.3 instead of exactly 2. Every twig is the thin end of a continuous path to the roots.
3. **A side branch is thickest where it leaves its parent.** It is set into the trunk as a sleeve: the branch's own wood turns down and wraps its base as a collar, and trunk wood wraps over that collar every year. A swelling underneath (the branch collar) and usually a raised ridge of bark on top (the branch bark ridge) mark the junction.
4. **Healthy crowns end in a network of long shoots; stressed ones don't.** Roloff's four vitality stages run from a net of long shoots at the crown edge (healthy) to spiky "bottle-brush" tips, then bushy chains of short shoots, then dieback and a shrinking crown.

**Terms used below.** *Acrotony*: side branches strongest near the tip of the parent shoot. *Orthotropic/plagiotropic*: growing upright/growing sideways. *Long shoot/short shoot*: a year's extension that is long and carries branches versus a stubby one. *Epicormic shoot*: a shoot from a dormant bud on an old trunk or limb (German *Wasserreiser*). *Reiteration*: the tree repeating its own basic architecture as a new sub-crown. *Retrenchment*: natural shrinking of an old crown. *Cladoptosis*: a tree's regular shedding of twigs at an abscission layer. *Sapwood/heartwood*: conducting outer wood/non-conducting inner wood.

## 1. How a tree is built

- **Growth rules.** Branches that develop mostly in the distal part of a parent shoot (acrotony) are what give a tree its tree-like rather than bushy habit. Upright (orthotropic) axes "are generally associated with plant skeleton construction." Sideways (plagiotropic) axes explore horizontal space and carry leaves and flowers. If a shoot's tip dies, aborts or turns into a flower, one, two or more branches take over below it (sympodial branching). A string of such takeovers can still look like one straight axis.
- **Limbs, branches, twigs.** Branches carry branches, and those carry twigs; in sympodial trees the steps pile up quickly. **General knowledge:** a mature broadleaved crown commonly has five or more such steps from trunk to this year's twig; I found no source that counts them species by species. Seen from any distance, only the trunk and the first limbs or two read as separate shapes; the finer branching merges into the crown's texture and the ragged edge of its outline.
- **Crowns within the crown.** As a crown matures, big limbs grow crowns of their own, each shaped by where it sits in the tree; this "sequential" reiteration is a normal part of crown construction. After damage, dormant buds produce "traumatic" reiteration: new small crowns on the wounded frame. **General knowledge:** an old crown therefore reads as a few uneven masses, not one even dome.
- **Long shoots and short shoots set the crown edge.** In a vigorous tree the leader and some side shoots at the top are long shoots, making a "network structure" that extends the crown. Next comes a "spikey outline," with bottle-brush tips of long leaders carrying only short side shoots. Then a "short shoot-mode" with "bushy structure, on hold." Last is "retraction mode": "leader die-back, crown reduction". Roloff measured these stages on 100- to 160-year-old beech. He sorts species by life expectancy. Short-lived (80–"}

{"id": "tree-structure", "title": "Tree structure and species", "page": 2, "pages": 4, "next_page": 3, "text": "100 years) includes alder and birch. Medium-lived (150–300) includes beech, spruce, pine and white willow. Long-lived (over 400) includes lime and oak.
- **What distress looks like.** In an ancient tree the outer crown shrinks episodically, and new epicormic shoots grow in the mid and lower crown. Old trees survive through epicormic growth, adventitious rooting, layering and suckering. *My inference:* a crown whose every limb is covered in straight upright shoots reads as a tree reacting to heavy damage or cutting. A healthy mature crown edge is a fine net of long shoots.

## 2. How branches taper and join

- **The branch-area rule.** A mother branch of diameter *d* splitting into daughters *dᵢ* obeys *d*^Δ = Σ *dᵢ*^Δ on average. Measured Δ is between 1.8 and 2.3 for many species (Δ = 2 means cross-sectional area is conserved). *Arithmetic from the rule:* with Δ = 2, two equal daughters are each about 0.71 of the mother's diameter. A daughter with a quarter of the area has half the diameter, and the mother continuing past it drops only to about 0.87 of its former diameter.
- **Why: two explanations.** The *pipe model* (Shinozaki et al. 1964) pictures a tree as a bundle of unit pipes, each connecting a set of leaves to the roots. So the stem area at a height tracks the leaves above it. Below the crown, the pipes of branches long since shed stay in the trunk as "disused pipes." That is why trunks keep thickening toward the base even where no branches remain. Eloy objects that the conducting sapwood can be as little as 5% of a mature trunk's cross-section. He shows instead that the rule follows if a self-similar tree skeleton sizes its diameters to resist wind. Whatever the cause, cross-sections sum roughly at forks.
- **When the rule bends.** Models depart from the rule as side branches get heavier or leave at wider angles. In real branches the departure is small. Beech branches fit a constant-stress design best; fir branches often follow the area rule. *My inference:* a heavy, near-horizontal limb is somewhat thicker at its base than the area rule alone would give.
- **What a junction is.** The cambium runs continuously from trunk to branch. In the upper junction, though, its cells are oriented at "approximately right angles" to the normal direction. Early in the season the branch xylem turns downward at the branch base and "encircles it to form a collar." Later in the season a collar of trunk xylem envelops it. "The branch is structurally attached to the trunk by a series of trunk collars that envelop the branch collars every growing season." Water enters and leaves the branch through the branch collar. Outwardly there is a branch collar on the underside of the branch base and a branch bark ridge on top, running roughly parallel to the branch angle.
- **Why a side branch never starts thinner than it is farther out.** *My inference, from and:* at its base a branch carries the pipes for every leaf beyond it, and each year's collar adds wood there first. Its cross-section therefore shrinks outward, stepwise at each fork and gradually between forks, and never the other way. A branch drawn as a constant-width rod, or narrower where it leaves the trunk, contradicts both.
- **Angle of attachment.** Wide, U-shaped unions are strong. Narrow V-shaped unions "often form included bark," a wedge of inward-rolled bark between two stems. Codominant stems of about equal size from one point often do the same. When a leader is damaged, several branches may become codominant.
- **Dead branches and stubs.** Around a dead branch, the collar and branch bark ridge "continue to grow" and can be told apart from the dead wood. *General knowledge:* over years a living collar can form a sleeve around a dead stub.
- **Twigs end in buds.** Each twig is the current year's shoot and ends in a terminal or false-terminal bud. Buds sit in the leaf scars along it (species details in §3). Nothing in a tree floats. Every twig connects through its pare"}

## 3. The species

### 3.1 Alder (*Alnus glutinosa*, black alder)

- **Habit.** Short-lived (normally about 60 years, maximum about 160), 10–25 m, on riverbanks, lake shores and marshes. The crown is narrow and upright. Shaded branches die off, so the live crown shrinks relative to the tree. It can be coppiced.
- **Twigs, catkins and cones.** Young twigs are green and sticky. Buds are stalked, purplish brown and somewhat three-sided. Catkins form in autumn and open the next spring. The fruits are small woody "cones" that stay on through winter and release seed gradually.
- **Bark.** Brown and smooth at first, then darker, rough and fissured. Later gray-brown with small broken patches.
- **Damage.** *Phytophthora* disease kills first the fine branches, then the larger ones.

### 3.2 Beech (*Fagus sylvatica*)

- **Habit.** Usually single-stemmed, with silver-gray bark. Typical life span 150–300 years. It keeps growing fast into late maturity and is the most shade-tolerant broadleaf in its range. A stocky trunk and round crown.
- **Twigs and buds.** Twigs are "slender, zigzag, light brown." Buds are long (about 2.5 cm), slender and "widely divergent from stems". Beech was Roloff's model species for the long-shoot/short-shoot vitality stages.
- **Bark.** "Smooth, thin, and dark gray-blue … smooth even on the largest stems, may be mottled". The thin bark protects poorly against fire and stripping.
- **Taper.** Japanese beech branches fit a uniform-stress design best.

### 3.3 Birch (*Betula pendula*, silver; *B. pubescens*, downy)

- **Habit.** Short-lived (commonly 90–100 years, rarely 150), relatively small, with a light canopy. The crown is open and pyramidal, "with distinctly drooping fine branches". In *B. pendula* the branches droop; in *B. pubescens* they grow upward or horizontally.
- **Twigs.** "Slender, reddish brown … noticeably drooping," with slender pointed buds.
- **Bark.** Brown when young, then "silvery-white, with horizontal dark grey lenticels, that with age darkens and develops fissures." Young trees show dark scars where shoots dropped. At the base the tree "develops thick bark which splits into narrow, vertical furrows which are nearly black".

### 3.4 Lime (*Tilia cordata*, small-leaved; *T. platyphyllos*, large-leaved)

- **Habit.** 30–40 m, with straight trunks up to about 1 m. Crowns are "quite neat and narrow, becoming untidier as they age," with a branch-free trunk of 10–15 m possible. Both species are largely free of suckers and epicormic growth, unlike the hybrid common lime. Open-grown trees are dense and round, and become as wide as tall.
- **Twigs and buds.** "Slender, zigzag, green-brown or red-tinged (particularly in the winter)." The terminal bud is false; buds are plump with one side bulging.
- **Bark.** Gray or brown, with shallow furrows and flat ridges. "Numerous burls and sprouts often found around the base".
- **Old limes.** They live over 1000 years even when coppiced. Very old stools may have lost their heartwood to rot. Limes were coppiced for long straight poles and can be pollarded.

### 3.5 Oak (*Quercus robur*, pedunculate; *Q. petraea*, sessile)

- **Habit.** In *Q. robur* the main trunk "tends to disappear in the crown, developing irregular boughs with twisting branches." *Q. petraea* usually keeps a main stem with boughs that gradually decrease in size. Heights are usually about 30 m, with diameters up to 1 m. Individuals can live over 1000 years and reach 3–4 m in diameter. The crown is round.
- **Twigs and buds.** Twigs are moderate in thickness and yellow-brown. Buds are "angled, short and round". **General knowledge:** oak buds cluster at the shoot tip, so several shoots start from one point, which gives oak its crooked, clustered branching.
- **Twig shedding (cladoptosis).** In cladoptosis an abscission layer forms and the twig "is shed cleanly," as leaves are. In oak, most shed twigs are one year old and leafless."}

In a 165-year-old stand, weak shoots had 27% lower hydraulic conductance, with bottlenecks at nodes and abscission zones.
- **Bark.** Gray and fissured into rectangular elongated blocks, thicker in *Q. robur*. "Deeply fissured with age".
- **Old and damaged oaks.** Oaks coppice and pollard easily. Lateral epicormic shoots leave knots in the wood. Ancient oaks retrench: the crown shrinks through dieback and branch loss ("growing downwards"). The trunk is very wide for the species and very likely hollow, and the tree may live on for centuries. In natural retrenchment, single branches die back while the rest of the crown stays healthy. Serious disease looks different.

### 3.6 Scots pine (*Pinus sylvestris*)

- **Habit.** 23–27 m on average, sometimes over 40 m. It lives 400 years or more. Crowns are rounded when young and round-topped when old. The trunk is often twisted, depending on seed origin. In some conifers, flattening and broadening of the crown may be the only sign of old-age retrenchment.
- **Bark.** The upper stem is "a distinct reddish-orange," while the lower part is "furrowed brown to grey-brown and becomes deeply fissured". "Upper crowns always show orange peeling bark".
- **Needles.** In pairs, twisted.

### 3.7 Norway spruce (*Picea abies*)

- **Habit.** A straight, regular trunk up to 50–60 m, usually living 200–300 years. "The crown is regularly conic, columnar, with whorled, short and stout branches, the upper level ascending and the lower drooping". Free-standing trees keep green branches down to the ground. Branches are inclined to hanging, as an adaptation to snow load.
- **Branching types.** Young spruces branch in flat "plates" up to about 20 years. After that they develop either the *Plattenfichte* type, with horizontal second-order branches, or the *Kammfichte* ("comb spruce") type, whose second- and higher-order branches hang down like a fringe. A third type is the *Bürstenfichte* ("brush spruce"). Comb spruces dominate on well-supplied sites. Plate spruces dominate on poor bogs and at extreme altitudes.
- **Bark.** Orange-brown. Red-brown and scaly, later gray with flaking scales or plates. Drops of resin are common on trunk and branches.

### 3.8 Willow (white willow, *Salix alba*; other tree willows)

- **The tree.** A fast-growing tree of riverbanks and floodplains, very tolerant of flooding. It "can readily reproduce from suckers or from adventitious roots". The bark is dark gray and deeply fissured with corky ridges. The narrow leaves are silver-gray, and white willow is "cultivated as osiers, characterised by having pliable branches". Medium-lived.

{"id": "oil-blending", "title": "Blending at the easel", "page": 1, "pages": 1, "next_page": null, "text": "## Blending

- **Blend inside one passage.** Shape the mask like the passage, with its
  edge where the paint already matches. Keep everything you want to keep
  outside the mask, dry shapes included: the blender carries wet paint onto
  them.
- **Look after each pass.** The blender lifts paint as it moves it. When
  darks go pale, texture flattens or the weave shows through, stop.
- **A seam that keeps coming back** needs another method. A smaller patch
  blended again rebuilds the box. Try something else across the whole
  transition on the scratch canvas: a thin tint of the original recipe,
  interlocking strokes of the two neighboring colors over dry paint, or the
  connected passage repainted up to its natural edges.
"}

{"id": "oil-ground", "title": "Oil ground handling at the easel", "page": 1, "pages": 1, "next_page": null, "text": "## Ground

- An **oil ground** (the default) absorbs nothing: paint stays open and
  glossy longer. An **absorbent ground** (`absorbent=true`) drinks the oil of
  thin paint: matte, lean, quick to set, colors that sit on the surface;
  thick paint is barely touched. Choose before you start: it is the
  canvas's character.
- A **toned ground** (a little ochre, umber or black in the white) sets the
  middle value from the first stroke; a white ground keeps everything high
  in key and lets thin paint glow.
"}

{"id": "oil-glazes", "title": "Glazing and scumbling at the easel", "page": 1, "pages": 1, "next_page": null, "text": "## Glazing and scumbling (over dry paint)

- **Glaze**: a transparent paint (lakes, viridian, ultramarine, a little of
  anything) with plenty of medium (0.7 to 0.85), `hand="glaze"`, over a dry
  passage. It deepens and saturates and lets the light underneath through;
  it rescues a chalky passage. Over impasto it pools in the valleys and
  thins on the ridges, which then shine through. Too much pigment, or any
  white, lays an opaque veil: try it small first. A glaze over the whole
  picture to pull it together has failed more often than it has worked.
- **Scumble**: light paint dragged thin over a dry darker passage, broken
  by the surface. A light load and
  `hand="scumble"` often lay opaque dabs. The veils that blended in came
  from paint thinned with `thinner`, laid in several light passes. Try it
  on the scratch canvas first.
- Glazes and scumbles want the passage under them **dry** (`wait` until
  `drying` says so): over open paint they just mix.
"}

-- limb edges
local function edges(pts, ws)
  local L, R = {}, {}
  for i=1,#pts do
    local a = pts[math.max(1,i-1)]; local b = pts[math.min(#pts,i+1)]
    local dx, dy = b[1]-a[1], b[2]-a[2]; local d = math.sqrt(dx*dx+dy*dy)
    local nx, ny = -dy/d, dx/d
    L[i] = {pts[i][1]+nx*ws[i]/2, pts[i][2]+ny*ws[i]/2}
    R[i] = {pts[i][1]-nx*ws[i]/2, pts[i][2]-ny*ws[i]/2}
  end
  return L, R
end
local hb = pencil("HB")
for k, br in pairs(tree) do

function sprout(limb, pl, opts)
  opts = opts or {}
  local pts, ws = limb[1], limb[2]
  local spacing = opts.spacing or 30
  local acc = rand(0, spacing)
  for i=1,#pts-1 do
    local x0,y0,x1,y1 = pts[i][1],pts[i][2],pts[i+1][1],pts[i+1][2]
    local dx,dy = x1-x0, y1-y0
    local d = math.sqrt(dx*dx+dy*dy)
    local la = math.atan(dy, dx)
    local s = 0
    while true do
      local step = spacing*rand(0.6,1.4)
      if acc + (d - s) < step then acc = acc + (d - s); break end
      s = s + (step - acc); acc = 0
      local t = s/d
      local wl = lerp(ws[i], ws[i+1], t)
      if wl < (opts.minw or 3) then goto cont end
      do
        local x, y = x0 + dx*t, y0 + dy*t
        local side = (math.random() < 0.5) and -1 or 1
        local a = la + side*rand(0.5, 1.2)
        -- bias upward
        a = a + 0.25*((-math.pi/2) - a)
        local bw = math.min(4.5, wl*rand(0.3, 0.5))
        local ln = (opts.len or 45) * rand(0.6, 1.3) * math.min(1.4, 0.6 + wl/15)
        -- start slightly inside the limb
        local ox, oy = x + math.cos(a)*wl*0.3, y + math.sin(a)*wl*0.3
        twig(ox, oy, a, ln, bw, opts.depth or 2, pl)
      end
      ::cont::
    end
  end
end

function sprout3(limb, pl, opts)
  opts = opts or {}
  local pts, ws = limb[1], limb[2]
  local spacing = opts.spacing or 30
  local acc = rand(0, spacing)
  for i=1,#pts-1 do
    local x0,y0,x1,y1 = pts[i][1],pts[i][2],pts[i+1][1],pts[i+1][2]

    while true do
      local step = spacing*rand(0.6,1.4)
      if acc + (d - s) < step then acc = acc + (d - s); break end
      s = s + (step - acc); acc = 0
      local t = s/d

      if wl >= (opts.minw or 3) then

        local side = (math.sin(up1) < math.sin(up2)) and -1 or 1
        if math.random() < 0.25 then side = -side end
        local a = la + side*rand(0.5, 1.1)
        a = a + 0.2*((-math.pi/2) - a)
        local bw = math.min(3.0, wl*rand(0.3, 0.45))
        local ln = (opts.len or 30) * rand(0.6, 1.3)
        local ox, oy = x + math.cos(a)*wl*0.35, y + math.sin(a)*wl*0.35
        zig2(ox, oy, a, ln, bw, opts.depth or 1, pl)

cl3 = pile{{"lead white",1.4},{"smalt",0.6},{"raw umber",0.4},{"rose madder",0.1},{"Naples yellow",0.3}, thinner=0.35, name="cl3"}
function cloud_lens(x0, x1, y, th, seed)
  local pts = {}
  local n = 14
  for i=0,n do
    local t = i/n
    local x = lerp(x0, x1, t)
    local h = th * math.sin(math.pi*t)^0.6 * (0.7 + 0.6*noise{seed=seed, period=60}:at01(x, y))
    pts[#pts+1] = {x, y - h*0.65}
  end
  for i=n,0,-1 do
    local t = i/n
    local x = lerp(x0, x1, t)
    local h = th * math.sin(math.pi*t)^0.8
    pts[#pts+1] = {x, y + h*0.35}
  end
  return poly(pts, true)
end
local c1 = cloud_lens(560, 990, 385, 9, 1) + cloud_lens(640, 900, 402, 6, 2) + cloud_lens(700, 1000, 368, 5, 3)
work(c1, {hand="body", tool="filbert 5", pile=cl3, angle=0, ruler=true, coverage=2, fill=true, clip=c1:grow(1), length={30,90}, seed=5})

arguments.lua:
local k = knife{width=9}
for _, s in ipairs(sec) do
  local pts = {}
  -- start a little away from the parent limb
  local x0,y0,x1,y1 = s[1][1], s[1][2], s[2][1], s[2][2]
  local dx,dy = x1-x0, y1-y0; local d = math.sqrt(dx*dx+dy*dy)
  local off = math.min(0.6, (s.w[1]*0.9 + 3)/d)
  pts[1] = {x0+dx*off, y0+dy*off}
  for i=2,#s do pts[#pts+1] = {s[i][1], s[i][2]} end
  -- extend past the tip
  local a,b = s[#s-1], s[#s]
  local ex,ey = b[1]-a[1], b[2]-a[2]; local el = math.sqrt(ex*ex+ey*ey)
  pts[#pts+1] = {b[1]+ex/el*8, b[2]+ey/el*8}
  k:scrape(pts, {pressure=1})
  k:wipe()
  k:scrape(pts, {pressure=1})
  k:wipe()
end

function crooked(x, y, ang, len, w0, w1, jit)
  jit = jit or 0.38
  local pts, ws = {{x,y}}, {w0}
  local n = math.max(3, math.floor(len/9 + 0.5))
  local a = ang
  local cx, cy = x, y
  for i=1,n do
    local seg = len/n * rand(0.75, 1.25)
    a = a + randn(0, jit)
    a = a + 0.35*(ang - a) + 0.05*((-math.pi/2) - a)
    cx, cy = cx + seg*math.cos(a), cy + seg*math.sin(a)
    pts[#pts+1] = {cx, cy}
    ws[#ws+1] = lerp(w0, w1, (i/n)^0.8)
  end
  return pts, ws
end
local function along(pts, ws, fn, spacing, minw)
  local acc = rand(0.3, 1.0)*spacing
  for i=1,#pts-1 do
    local x0,y0,x1,y1 = pts[i][1],pts[i][2],pts[i+1][1],pts[i+1][2]
    local dx,dy = x1-x0, y1-y0
    local d = math.sqrt(dx*dx+dy*dy)
    local la = math.atan(dy, dx)
    local s = acc
    while s < d do
      local t = s/d
      local wl = lerp(ws[i], ws[i+1], t)
      if wl >= minw then fn(x0+dx*t, y0+dy*t, la, wl, i + t) end
      s = s + spacing*rand(0.6, 1.4)
    end
    acc = s - d
  end
end
local function upside(la)
  local s1 = la - math.pi/2
  return (math.sin(s1) < 0) and -1 or 1
end
function grow_crown(limbs, opts)
  local out = {}
  for li, L in ipairs(limbs) do
    along(L[1], L[2], function(x, y, la, wl, pos)
      local side = upside(la); if math.random() < 0.3 then side = -side end
      local a = la + side*rand(0.45, 1.05)
      a = a + 0.25*((-math.pi/2) - a)
      local w0 = math.min(opts.maxw or 6, wl*rand(0.4, 0.6))
      local len = rand(0.7, 1.3) * (opts.len or 45) * math.min(1.5, 0.5 + wl/12)

I'll build a clump_trees function painting overlapping ellipses of varying size as crowns along the band, flat-bottomed, layered over the existing wet lozenges so they merge naturally, with roughened edges for texture.

arguments.lua:
function clump_trees(x0, x1, yb, hmin, hmax, seed)
  local m = rect(x0, yb - hmin*0.6, x1 - x0, hmin*0.6 + 0.5)
  local x = x0 + rand(0, 2)
  while x < x1 do
    local t = (x - x0)/(x1 - x0)
    local env = 0.45 + 0.55*math.sin(math.pi*t)^0.5
    local h = rand(hmin, hmax) * env
    local rx = h*rand(0.35, 0.6)
    m = m + ellipse(x, yb - h + h*0.45, rx, h*0.5)
    x = x + rx*rand(0.9, 1.6)
  end
  return m:roughen(0.5, 2.5, seed)
end

content.text:
From the critic's visit you asked for:

Notes for the painter, day 56: answers to your four questions and what I'd change

The large shapes already work. The light sky against the dark land reads right away. The dusk gradient from smalt down to cream is the best passage in the picture, and the day-16 restatement left the zenith calm with no seam. The little spire is well judged: small and hazy, the same value as the far hills. Most of what I'd change is in the land and the tree. Here it is in order of importance, with your four questions answered along the way.

**1. The middle plain: the copses are what break the depth (your question 2).**
Look at the two copses in the value view: the one at x 640–720, y ~500, and the clump at x 890–1000, y ~490. They're the same value and both have hard edges, with bottoms cut flat as if by a ruler. The right one is nearer the horizon, so it's farther away, yet it isn't any lighter. Both are a good deal darker than the haze around them. That's why they look like cut-outs, small bushes a stone's throw off, when they should be woods a few kilometres away, and they flatten the plain around them.
- Scumble or glaze them toward the haze. The far clump should come close to the value of the far hills band. The nearer one can sit a step darker but still clearly lighter than the hill.
- Soften the bottom edges so they settle into the ground.

The plain itself (y 500–620) has a gentle gradient but nothing that recedes. Two things would build the space without any new objects:
- **Break up the lagoon.** At the horizon it's become one continuous strip of even thickness, from about x 520 to the right edge. In value it reads as a slit in the land, the ribbon problem again in a smaller form. Cut it into two or three lenses of different lengths, with low dark spits of land between them.
- **Add one nearer, larger water passage**, somewhere around y 540–570 on the right. Near water reflects higher sky, so make it a cooler, slightly bluer light than the cream far water. That warm-far, cool-near reflection is a strong depth cue, and it uses what you learned on day 13 (horizontal slivers, thin with distance).

There are already stray flecks there, ghosts of the old channel: x 880–980, y 530–570, and a light-blue speck right on the edge at x ~997, y ~555–565. Either build them into this pool or take them out. The one on the edge pulls the eye out of the frame.

**2. The figure (question 1).**
The scale is right, and its placement on the forward shoulder, apart from the trunk, is good. One fix: the far-hills contour runs across its neck at y ~456, so the head sits on the line. That tangency shrinks the figure, and the coat is set against the mid-grey hills instead of the glow you moved it for on day 6. Paint a shallow saddle into the far hills behind it, about 8–10 units deep over about 60 units of width, using your sky_fix glow mix. Then head and shoulders stand clear against the light. It's a small job with a big payoff, because the figure is the hinge of the picture.

**3. The oak (question 3): it reads as a fine dead tree, but not yet as an oak.**
Three things make it generic:
- **The trunk** is a parallel-sided column from y 480 to 360, like a post. Friedrich's oaks are squat and lumpy, with a swollen fork.
- **The crown** rises in a vase shape from a single fork. That's closer to an elm.
- **Every branch tip ends in the same motif:** a curled claw of two to four rigger hooks. On the far-left limb (x 80–130, y 250–300) they hang down like seaweed. That repetition is what gives the tree away as generic.

I wouldn't repaint it. Targeted changes:
- Break the trunk's contour with one or two bulges and a fuller fork. You can work from either side, cutting in with sky or adding tree paint.
- Put an abrupt kink into two of the main limbs, each with a short dead stub at the bend.
- Vary the tips. Leave some limbs ending blunt and broken, with nothing on them (stag-headed). Give only a few a dense, fine, angular mesh. Paint out the drooping curls.
- The right-hand stub at x 340–360, y 375 has a round, peg-like end. Shorten it and make the end splintered and jagged.

**4. The hill surface and shape.**
Look at the hill in the gallery and relief views. Because it's still wet, it may yet level, but right now it reads as a uniform crinkled leather: grey, wormy, with no direction. In raking light it also lifts the value, so the silhouette goes grey. It's the largest area in the picture, and the surface fights the glassy sky and the thin Friedrich method you planned. While it's still open, I'd do a flattening pass along the slope.

The contour is a near-perfect arc, like a burial mound. Where the crest crosses the lighter plain (x 230–460, and the right flank at 480–600), a few small breaks would loosen the arc and give the figure a scale reference: tussocks, a stone, a few heather tufts in silhouette. Also darken the hill slightly toward the bottom edge so the dome has some volume.

**5. The sky (question 4): yes to the cloud bands, but only low on the right, and only a few.**
Replace the stippled bits at x 680–830 and 900–1000, y 375–395. Up close they look like a halftone screen and don't match any other mark in the picture.
- Lay one or two long, thin, tapering bands parallel to the horizon, around y 385–415, using the calm ruler strokes that worked on day 16.
- Make them a violet-grey just darker than the glow.
- Keep them well clear of the moon and the zenith.

That also answers your other worry about the right side. It isn't too empty; emptiness suits this subject. What it needs is a little horizontal structure that echoes the horizon and carries the figure's gaze out to the moon. The bands and the reworked water do that without adding any objects.

**6. A small one for gallery light.**
The sky repair left of the trunk (x ~213–280, y ~375–403) shows as raised rectangles in relief and gallery light. You can't see it in flat view, but on a wall the square edges will show. If you can skim the ridges once it's hard, do; otherwise, keep any further patches soft-edged.

If you only have time for three of these, do the copse values, the saddle behind the figure, and the oak tips.

arguments.lua:
function copse_cover(x0, x1, yb, hmax, seed, extra)
  extra = extra or 1.5
  local m = rect(x0 - 3, yb - 2.5, (x1 - x0) + 7, 4.2)
  local x = x0 - 2
  while x < x1 + 4 do
    local t = clamp((x - x0)/(x1 - x0), 0, 1)
    local env = 0.45 + 0.55*math.sin(math.pi*t)^0.5
    local hneed = 1.05*hmax*env + extra
    local h = hneed * rand(1.0, 1.22)
    local rx = rand(2.5, 4.5) + h*0.25
    m = m + ellipse(x, yb - h + h*0.5, rx, h*0.5)
    x = x + rx*rand(0.6, 1.0)
  end
  return m:roughen(0.5, 2.5, seed)
end
cop_near = copse_cover(642, 715, 512.5, 13, 601)

arguments.lua:
t_twig = pile{{"raw umber",1.2},{"bone black",0.8},{"Prussian blue",0.08},{"red earth",0.05}, medium=0.15, name="t_twig"}
rg_s = brush{kind="rigger", width=1.6, point=1}
rd_m = brush{kind="round", width=4, point=1}
function angular_pts(x, y, ang, len, nseg, jit, upb)
  local nodes = {{x, y}}
  local a = ang
  local cx, cy = x, y
  for i=1,nseg do
    local seg = len/nseg * rand(0.7, 1.3)
    a = a + randn(0, jit)
    a = a + upb*((-math.pi/2) - a) + 0.3*(ang - a)
    cx, cy = cx + seg*math.cos(a), cy + seg*math.sin(a)
    nodes[#nodes+1] = {cx, cy, a}
  end
  return nodes
end
function draw_angular(br, nodes, w0, pl)
  -- densify each straight segment so the smooth gesture stays angular
  local pts = {}
  local n = #nodes
  for i=1,n-1 do
    local a, b = nodes[i], nodes[i+1]
    for k=0,2 do
      local t = k/3
      local tt = ((i-1) + t)/(n-1)
      local w = w0*(1 - 0.75*tt)
      local p = math.max(0.3, br:pressure_for(math.max(w, 0.7)))
      pts[#pts+1] = {lerp(a[1], b[1], t), lerp(a[2], b[2], t), p}
    end
  end
  pts[#pts+1] = {nodes[n][1], nodes[n][2], 0.08}
  if br:fullness() < 0.45 then br:reload(pl, 0.75) end
  br:gesture(pts, {wobble=0.1, ramps={0.02, 0.25}})
end
function oak_spray(x, y, ang, len, w, depth, pl)
  local br = (w > 1.7) and rd_m or rg_s
  local nodes = angular_pts(x, y, ang, len, math.random(2, 4), 0.55, 0.12)
  draw_angular(br, nodes, w, pl)
  if depth > 0 then
    -- shoots cluster at the tip and at one node
    local tip = nodes[#nodes]
    local k = math.random(2, 3)
    for j=1,k do
      oak_spray(tip[1], tip[2], tip[3] + randn(0, 0.7), len*rand(0.35, 0.6), math.max(0.8, w*0.6), depth-1, pl)
    end
    if #nodes > 2 and math.random() < 0.6 then
      local nd = nodes[math.random(2, #nodes-1)]
      local s = (math.random()<0.5) and -1 or 1
      oak_spray(nd[1], nd[2], nd[3] + s*rand(0.5, 1.1), len*rand(0.35, 0.55), math.max(0.8, w*0.55), depth-1, pl)
    end
  end
end

arguments.lua:
t_twig = pile{{"raw umber",1.2},{"bone black",0.8},{"Prussian blue",0.08},{"red earth",0.05}, medium=0.15, name="t_twig"}
rg_s = brush{kind="rigger", width=1.6, point=1}
rd_m = brush{kind="round", width=4, point=1}
function angular_pts(x, y, ang, len, nseg, jit, upb)
  local nodes = {{x, y, ang}}
  local a = ang
  local cx, cy = x, y
  for i=1,nseg do
    local seg = len/nseg * rand(0.7, 1.3)
    a = a + randn(0, jit)
    a = a + upb*((-math.pi/2) - a) + 0.3*(ang - a)
    cx, cy = cx + seg*math.cos(a), cy + seg*math.sin(a)
    nodes[#nodes+1] = {cx, cy, a}
  end
  return nodes
end
function draw_angular(br, nodes, w0, pl)
  local pts = {}
  local n = #nodes
  for i=1,n-1 do
    local a, b = nodes[i], nodes[i+1]
    for k=0,2 do
      local t = k/3
      local tt = ((i-1) + t)/(n-1)
      local w = w0*(1 - 0.75*tt)
      local p = math.max(0.3, br:pressure_for(math.max(w, 0.7)))
      pts[#pts+1] = {lerp(a[1], b[1], t), lerp(a[2], b[2], t), p}
    end
  end
  pts[#pts+1] = {nodes[n][1], nodes[n][2], 0.08}
  if br:fullness() < 0.45 then br:reload(pl, 0.75) end
  br:gesture(pts, {wobble=0.1, ramps={0.02, 0.25}})
end
function oak_spray(x, y, ang, len, w, depth, pl)
  local br = (w > 1.7) and rd_m or rg_s
  local nodes = angular_pts(x, y, ang, len, math.random(2, 3), 0.45, 0.1)
  draw_angular(br, nodes, w, pl)
  if depth > 0 then

The hill is the dominant shape in the composition so it's worth the careful pass, and I still plan to add heather tufts along the crest silhouette afterward.

For spacing the overlay strokes, I'm working out rows offset progressively downward from the hill's contour, sampling x positions across the canvas and skipping the segment where the tree trunk sits so the stroke doesn't collide with its root flare near the base.

There's also a figure standing further right whose feet sit just above the contour line, so I need to skip that x-range on the first row to avoid cutting through its legs. I'm also keeping in mind the knife-edge logic—how the blade rides over high points and levels the paint underneath it, leaving a flat ridge, which only matters for wet paint and not here since this is dry.

Loading each path with paint, I should limit stroke length to around 200 units with reloads in between, since longer strokes would run dry; the reload points will naturally create small torn edges where the blade lifts off, so I'll stagger those breaks across overlapping rows at 22-unit spacing so they don't line up. The blend created a harsh rectangular edge where it meets the dry lower hill — since blending can't lift paint from dry areas but can still deposit wet pigment onto them, a wider, softer blend might spread that dark film thin enough to disguise the boundary.

content.text:
From the critic's visit you asked for:

The picture works. A dark oak and a small figure against a long cream glow, the moon set off in a big empty blue, a plain going back in haze: it reads at once as a Friedrich evening. The upper sky is calm now, the saddle puts the figure's head against the light, and the copses and lagoon sit back in the haze. What still weakens it, in order:

**1. The hill is one flat value, and that weakens the picture most.**
The darkness isn't the problem. A dark foreground under a light sky is the idea of the picture. The problem is that it's the same dark everywhere.
- **No gradient.** In value mode the hill is one even dark from the crest at y~485 down to the bottom edge, and on into the foreground shelf at lower right. Your "darker toward the bottom" didn't register at all.
- **Dead in the gallery light.** The hill looks like flat brown leather with an even crinkle all over. Nothing in it says "near" or "far", "top" or "front".
- **A compass arc.** Its left profile, from (0,520) up to the trunk, is a perfectly smooth arc. Smooth outline plus even value makes a stage flat: the sky and plain go back in space, and the hill sits in front of them like a paper cutout.
- **The tussocks don't read.** The crest ones are too small to see at viewing distance. The two grey marks on the meadow just above the crest (x 115–160, y 488–500) look like smudges, not bushes.

What I would do, with a few broad moves and no local patching:
- **Darken the near ground.** Lay one thin dark glaze over the dry hill and shelf (your g_tree mix works) along the whole bottom edge. Load it fully at y 714 and fade it to nothing by about y 590. Then the near ground is a step darker than the body of the hill, and there's depth inside the dark. There's no light paint down there, so blending it won't drag anything out.
- **Cool the top of the hill.** A very thin cool scumble (hb_main with a little d2) on the top plane, from the crest down 30–40 units, mostly left of the figure. The top of a backlit mound catches a little skylight, and that's what makes it turn. Keep it to half a step of value at most.
- **Break the arc.** Add one slight swell or dip in the left profile, and two or three tussocks big enough to read against the meadow (10–15 units wide, dark, ragged tops). Then either turn the two smudges into something that clearly sits on the crest, or cover them with meadow.

Keep it empty otherwise. No rocks or paths: the emptiness is right, the flatness isn't.

**2. The right-hand slope reads as an edge, not as a form.**
It's a clean diagonal from the figure's shoulder (x~520) down to about (690,600), and it's as dark as the shelf in front of it, so nothing says it turns or goes back. The "banks" along it read in value mode as a band of dark spots following the outline, like leopard print, not ground.
- **Separate it from the shelf.** The top of the slope near the figure is farther away than the shelf at the bottom. Leave it a hair lighter and cooler, and let the bottom glaze from point 1 darken the lower front. That depth difference does most of the work.
- **Turn the spots into contours.** Restate the spots as a few long, low marks that run across the slope's face along its contour. A bank is a ledge, not a dot.
- **Give the edge scale.** A few small tufts on the slope's outline against the lighter plain, getting smaller toward the figure.

**3. The twig sprays read as a repeated "v", as you suspected.**
In crop 440,170,590,300 almost every branch end on the right side of the crown has the same small, even, upward fork, about 8 units, ink-dark, crisp. The sprouts along the limbs repeat the same fork. At full view the crown edge is studded with dozens of identical little crow's feet. The eye counts them as a pattern, and the tree starts to look illustrated rather than grown.

The top centre (x 320–440, y 95–185) is better because the forks overlap and mass. On the upper limbs the bare, broken-off tops work too: the stag-head reads there.

Your journal says that patching sky over twigs makes squares, so don't remove the forks. Make them stop being the unit the eye counts, by adding:
- **Vary the size of the clusters a lot.** On perhaps half the tips, add a second and third generation of short, crooked, elbowed twiglets. Make each fork unequal: a leader carries on and the side shoot leaves at a wide angle, often near horizontal. Oak is zig-zag and spreading, not candelabra. Those tips become dense, irregular clusters of different sizes, and the old "v" disappears inside them. Leave the others alone. A few limbs can end blunt, with nothing.
- **Make the outer twigs lighter than the limbs.** Twigs this fine, seen against a bright sky, show as a mid-tone, not as black lines. Your haze_twig mix is the right colour, but 187 hairs spread over the whole crown read as scattered scratches. Concentrate them around the clusters on the outer edge of the crown (upper right and top), so the crown dissolves into a tone at its edge instead of ending in crisp black ticks.
- **The left limb tip** (x 65–110, y 265–290) has the worst spot. It ends in a zig-zag shaped like a "3", with a separate piece floating just left of it that isn't joined to anything. Connect the piece to the limb with a crooked link and fold both into one irregular cluster.

**4. Smaller things, all near where the eye goes:**
- **The far ridge just right of the figure** (x 500–525, y 455–462) still has square steps from the f_land2 rectangles. It's right beside the figure's head. Work the ridge into one continuous, slightly irregular line with a small detail brush.
- **Left of the trunk base** (x 245–262, y 470–486) there's a paler rectangle with a hard vertical edge against the root flare. Cover it with meadow, or let the root flare spread out over it.
- **Old patches show in the gallery and raking light**: circles at x 100–195, y 280–355 and rectangles at x 215–290 and 335–360, y 365–395. This is ridge texture, not colour; you can't see it in daylight. Patching will only add more. The only real cure is restating the whole low-sky band from edge to edge, as you did up top. I'd treat that as optional and do it last, if at all.

If you only do one thing, do the glaze on the near ground and the cool on the top of the hill. That is what turns the dark lower third from a cut-out into ground the figure is standing on.

  local y = hy(x) + 1

    local a = -math.pi/2 + randn(0, 0.35)

function zigzag(br, x, y, ang, len, p0, pl)
  local n = math.random(3, 5)
  local pts = {{x, y, p0}}
  local a = ang
  local cx, cy = x, y
  local nodes = {}
  local sgn = (math.random() < 0.5) and -1 or 1
  for i=1,n do
    a = ang + sgn*rand(0.25, 0.55) + randn(0, 0.12)
    sgn = -sgn
    local seg = len/n * rand(0.7, 1.3)
    cx, cy = cx + seg*math.cos(a), cy + seg*math.sin(a)
    pts[#pts+1] = {cx, cy, (i==n) and 0.04 or lerp(p0, 0.28, i/n)}
    nodes[#nodes+1] = {cx, cy, a}
  end
  if br:fullness() < 0.4 then br:reload(pl, 0.65) end
  br:gesture(pts, {wobble=0.05, ramps={0.02, 0.35}})
  return nodes
end
function cluster(x, y, ang, size, gens, pl, br)
  br = br or rg_s
  local nodes = zigzag(br, x, y, ang + randn(0, 0.2), size, 0.45, pl)
  if gens <= 0 then return end
  for i, nd in ipairs(nodes) do
    if i < #nodes and math.random() < 0.65 then
      local side = (math.random()<0.5) and -1 or 1
      -- wide, often near-horizontal side shoots
      local sa = nd[3] + side*rand(0.8, 1.4)
      sa = sa + 0.25*((side > 0 and 0 or math.pi) - sa) * 0 
      cluster(nd[1], nd[2], sa, size*rand(0.4, 0.65), gens-1, pl, br)
    end
  end
  local tip = nodes[#nodes]
  if math.random() < 0.7 then cluster(tip[1], tip[2], tip[3] + randn(0, 0.5), size*rand(0.4, 0.6), gens-1, pl, br) end
end

arguments.text:
### Day 178-206: critic's second visit, responses
- Near-ground glaze g_near (black 1.2, umber .9, Prussian .08, medium .7), hand=glaze, load_at ramp from y 575 (0) to 705 (1), clipped to the hill below the crest: the dark now deepens toward the bottom edge; the hill has depth inside the dark. (Scratch first: a matching glaze over a dry dark body coat.)
- Top plane: cool_t (hb_main pigments + lw .35, smalt .3, cobalt .18, thinner .5), body filbert 7 following the slope, load fading over 38 units below the crest, stronger left of the figure; one blend pass. It reads as skylight on the top of the mound, but it left a speckled light lattice (thin light paint in the hollows of the old ridged texture). A thin g_hill2 glaze (medium .78) + a light dipped-rag wipe softened it. Still slightly speckled near the crest: accepted as the worn heath surface.
- Left profile: hyL() = hy with a 3.8-unit swell (x 25-125) and a slight dip (x 140-200); meadow repainted above, hill below. FAILED first: tussocks as big ellipse bodies + blades read as black blobs (scraped and wiped while open). WORKED: grass_clump = 13-35 rigger blades fanning from one base with a common lean; reads at viewing distance as tussocks.
- Crown: 52 'cluster' zig-zag twig systems (zigzag polyline alternating ±.25-.55 rad, side shoots at .8-1.4 rad = near-horizontal, 2 generations), weighted to the outer crown; then 57 lighter clusters in haze_twig on the outer edge. The repeated 'v' is now absorbed in irregular clusters of different size; the outer edge goes toward mid-tone.
- Fixes: left limb end reconnected with a crooked gesture (round 3 point 1) and folded into a cluster; root flare spread over the pale rectangle left of the trunk; small light specks on the meadow/crest covered with matching meadow piles (dry); trunk and lower limbs re-glazed with g_tree, load fading up (the earlier g_tree glaze had stopped at y 330 as a hard band visible in gallery light).

## Reflections and handoff (day 206)
The picture: an old stag-headed oak on a dark heath mound at dusk; a small figure in a greatcoat and cap with a stick stands on the shoulder of the mound, his head against the glow, looking out over a hazy marsh with a lagoon and pools catching the light, far blue hills with a church spire, thin violet strata low on the right, a young crescent moon and evening star in a big calm blue. I'm happy with the sky, the figure's placement, the far plain and the oak's silhouette. It reads as a quiet Friedrich evening.

Unresolved passages (if continuing):
- Low sky left of the trunk: old patch rectangles/circles show as raised texture in gallery/raking light only (x 100-195 y 280-355; x 215-290 and 335-360 y 365-395). Cure would be restating the whole low-sky band edge to edge (as was done for the upper sky); not attempted.
- Hill: still a slightly speckled light lattice on the top plane (from the cool scumble over ridged paint) and some light flecks along the right slope edge. The right slope reads as form but its face is still fairly uniform.
- Crown: the inner crown still has some small crisp forks; the outer edge is better.
- The legs of the figure are a touch warm/light against the coat.

Practical lessons (hypotheses unless noted as observed repeatedly):
- Observed repeatedly: small local sky patches never match a thin film over a glaze; restate the whole band edge to edge with the original recipe and handling (ruler broad strokes, load_at fade), clipped around protected shapes.
- Observed: ribbon() end discs (radius w/2) and masks used for protection can silently preserve a mistake; print mask:at() at the stubborn spot.
- Observed: a badger blend next to OPEN light paint drags it out into a rectangle; blend before placing light accents or after they dry.
- Observed: the knife's bead is a reservoir: wipe it between piles. Lua: guard loops that step `x = x1 - overlap` with a capped x1 (infinite loop -> chunk stopped).
- Observed: dipped rag (dip .95, fresh rag each pass, mask wipe) cleans open paint off a DRY underlayer well; a path wipe leaves streaks; paint 12+ h old and thick barely lifts.
- Observed: held piles (look hold) show the masstone thick; thin films over other colors come out different. Lay a 15-unit test stroke on the painting (or scratch) and judge it in a crop.
- Hypothesis: glazes over ridged dry body paint deepen without adding texture; light scumbles over the same ridges lodge in hollows and speckle.
- Branches: ribbon masks for limbs/secondaries + rigger gestures for twigs; avoid long smooth single gestures for branches (tentacles) and identical end motifs (counted as pattern).

content.text:
**Evening on the Heath (The Old Oak)**

An old oak stands dark against a dusk sky on a heath mound. Its crown is retrenched, the top limbs are dead and broken off, and the oak-like shoots cluster at the ends of the limbs. A small figure in a greatcoat and cap, seen from behind and leaning on a stick, stands on the mound's shoulder. I cut a low dip into the far hills behind him so that his head stands against the cream glow at the horizon. Below him a hazy marsh goes back to a lagoon that catches the last light, then to blue hills with a small church spire. Above, the sky shades from smalt blue to cream. It holds a young crescent moon, an evening star and a few thin violet strips of cloud low on the right. I worked the way Friedrich did: a warm knifed ground under a pale brushed one, a pencil drawing, thin layers, glazes, and small details added last over dry paint.

**Handoff (also in the journal):**
- **Still unresolved:**
  - In gallery or raking light you can still see the raised texture of old patches in the low sky left of the trunk. Restating that whole band from edge to edge would fix it; I didn't attempt it.
  - A cool scumble on the top of the mound left fine light speckles near the crest.
  - The right slope reads as a form, but its face is still fairly uniform.
  - Some small, crisp forks remain inside the crown.
- **Seen more than once:**
  - Painting small patches of sky never matched a thin film laid over a glaze. Restating the whole band with the original recipe and handling worked.
  - A badger blend next to light paint that was still wet dragged it out into a pale rectangle.
  - The paint on a knife carries over between piles, so wipe it in between.
  - A rag dipped in solvent, with a fresh one for each pass, cleans wet paint off a dry layer well.
- **Failed recipes:**
  - A water channel drawn as a band of even width.
  - Branches made as long, smooth single strokes; they looked like tentacles.
  - Small rectangular patches of sky laid over branch tips.
  - Tussocks made as ellipse shapes; they read as black blobs.
  - Smoothing the hill with a knife without wiping it between piles.
- **Hypotheses to test:**
  - Glazes over dry, ridged paint deepen it without adding texture, while light scumbles lodge in the hollows and speckle.
  - If a mistake survives repeated repainting, check whether a protection mask is preserving it. Here, the round end of a trunk mask kept a pale bowl under the trunk until I cut it.
